content.title: About
content.content: American reduced‑sodium cheese is a processed cheese made from cow’s milk with a lower salt content. It has a smooth, creamy texture and the classic buttery flavor of American cheese, but with significantly less sodium than the regular version.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sodium reduction is achieved through special processing techniques and salt substitutes.
American cheese is popular in burgers, sandwiches, and melt‑type snacks because it melts uniformly.
The lower salt level gives the cheese a longer shelf life compared with many natural cheeses.
It is sold in slices, blocks, or shredded form for convenient use.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Provides calcium that supports bone and teeth health.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Protein contributes to muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Includes vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Reduced salt is beneficial for people monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose, which may cause discomfort for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to this cheese.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Despite lower sodium, it still contains saturated fats and should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice for burgers, melt in sandwiches, add to pasta, salads, or use in sauces. It can also be shredded over dishes for a quick cheesy topping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Follow the “best‑by” date on the package; discard if you notice off‑odors, mold, or discoloration.

cookie-graham-cracker-with-chocolate-and.title: Graham Cracker Cookie with Chocolate and Marshmallow

content.title: About
content.content: The Graham Cracker Cookie with chocolate and marshmallow is a crunchy whole‑grain cracker topped with a layer of milk chocolate and a soft marshmallow filling. The flavor combines sweet chocolate notes, the mild caramelization of the graham cracker, and the airy sweetness of marshmallow.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Graham crackers were originally created in the United States in the early 20th century as a healthier alternative to sweets.
The chocolate‑marshmallow combination is a classic American treat, popular in s’mores.
Marshmallow inside the cookie makes the interior softer despite the crisp outer shell.
The chocolate used is typically milk chocolate, but dark chocolate can be used for a richer taste.
The cookie is often served as a snack with tea or coffee.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the cracker and sugar in the marshmallow quickly replenish glucose stores.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Whole‑grain graham crackers provide small amounts of iron, beneficial for blood formation.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Milk chocolate is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Sugar and chocolate promote serotonin production, improving mood.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The crunchy texture and sweet filling help create a feeling of fullness.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Graham crackers contain wheat, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Lactose and milk protein
items.content: Chocolate and marshmallow may contain lactose and milk proteins, which can trigger reactions in intolerant individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The cookie is relatively calorie‑dense, so moderate consumption is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, crumble it into ice cream, use it as a layer in desserts, or pair it with a hot beverage. For a softer texture, briefly warm it in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent chocolate bloom.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit salad is a mixture of fresh fruits, often featuring citrus fruits (oranges, mandarins, grapefruit, lemon) combined with other seasonal fruits and tossed with a light dressing made from salad sauce or mayonnaise. The dish offers a bright aroma, juicy taste, and works well as a snack or dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Citrus fruits are rich in vitamin C, which boosts immunity and improves skin health.
The combination of fruit and a light mayonnaise‑based dressing originated in the United States in the early 20th century.
Fruit salad is a popular holiday dish because its vivid colors create a festive atmosphere.
Many variations exist: honey, yogurt, nuts, mint, or ginger are often added for extra flavor.
When stored properly, the salad stays fresh for up to 24 hours; after that, the fruit may start to lose texture.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Citrus fruits and berries provide a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and fights free radicals.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fruits contain soluble and insoluble fiber that promotes healthy digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium found in bananas, oranges, and kiwi helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: A moderate portion delivers energy without excessive calories, making it suitable for weight management.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bananas, kiwi, and mango supply vitamins B6 and B9, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oranges, lemons, or grapefruit.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruits are naturally sweet; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acid from citrus can irritate sensitive tooth enamel and the stomach if consumed in excess.

items.title: Mayonnaise content
items.content: Traditional mayonnaise adds saturated fat and calories; a lighter yogurt‑based dressing can be used as an alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled; you can add mint, nuts, or seeds for crunch. It works as a light appetizer, a side to meat dishes, or a standalone dessert. For a lighter version, replace mayonnaise with a yogurt dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fruit salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing. Discard any fruit that has darkened or lost its fresh aroma.

hot-dog-sandwich-reduced-fat-on-wheat-bu.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, Reduced Fat, on Wheat Bun

content.title: About
content.content: The reduced‑fat hot dog sandwich is a classic hot dog made with lean meat patty served in a whole‑grain wheat bun. It contains less saturated fat while preserving the familiar taste and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lean patty is usually made from turkey or chicken breast, lowering the calorie count.
Whole‑grain wheat bun adds extra fiber and micronutrients.
The hot dog was invented in the United States in the late 19th century and quickly became a fast‑food staple.
Fat reduction is achieved by trimming visible fat and using leaner cuts of meat.
In some countries the reduced‑fat version is served with a yogurt‑based sauce instead of mayonnaise.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Reduced saturated fat helps maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Lean meat provides essential protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Fiber from whole‑grain bun
items.content: The wheat bun supplies dietary fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole grains are sources of B1, B2, B6 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The product contains iron, zinc and selenium, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Meat or gluten allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to meat proteins or gluten present in the wheat bun.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed meat products often contain salt; people monitoring sodium intake should be aware.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain versions may include nitrites or other preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the hot dog in an oven or on a grill so the bun stays crisp and the patty stays juicy. Add fresh vegetables, mustard, ketchup, or a yogurt‑based dip as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the ready‑to‑eat product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 3 days. Frozen versions can be stored for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: The diet Iced Tea / Lemonade drink is a refreshing, zero‑calorie blend of tea and lemonade, sweetened with artificial sweeteners. It combines the smooth flavor of cold tea with a bright citrus lemon note, contains no sugar and is suitable for low‑calorie diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink merges two popular flavors—black tea and lemonade—into one product.
Sweetening is done with sucralose or stevia, which have minimal impact on blood glucose.
Often includes lemon zest extract to retain aroma after pasteurization.
Diet versions frequently add vitamin C derived from lemon juice.
It is a popular summer alternative to sugary sodas.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: One serving contains fewer than 5 kcal, making it suitable for weight management.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Tea antioxidants
items.content: Black tea provides polyphenols that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Lemon juice supplies a modest amount of vitamin C, supporting immune function.

items.title: Sugar‑free
items.content: Absence of sugar makes the drink safe for people with diabetes when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some individuals may experience gastrointestinal discomfort from sucralose or stevia.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice increases acidity, which can irritate sensitive teeth or the stomach.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to tea components can occur.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Caffeine in tea may amplify the effects of certain stimulants or affect sleep.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve chilled; optionally add a lemon slice or fresh mint for extra aroma. Ideal as a refreshing snack between meals or as part of a diet plan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 2‑4 °C. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not freeze, as texture and flavor may change.

infant-formula-enfamil-gentlease-powder-.title: Enfamil Gentlease Infant Formula, Powder, Made with Baby Water

content.title: About
content.content: Enfamil Gentlease is an infant formula powder designed for babies from birth to 12 months. It combines partially hydrolyzed proteins, probiotics, and an optimal balance of fats, carbohydrates, and vitamins. Preparation uses specially purified baby water, ensuring a consistent and safe composition.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gentlease contains partially hydrolyzed proteins, which reduce the likelihood of colic and gas in infants.
The formula is enriched with pre‑biotics (FOS) that support the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.
It includes DHA and ARA – essential fatty acids for brain and eye development.
The product has undergone clinical trials confirming its hypoallergenic properties.
Each container yields about 800 ml of ready‑to‑feed formula, convenient for home use.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Partially hydrolyzed proteins and pre‑biotics help reduce colic, gas, and constipation.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA promote neuronal connections and visual function.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, E and zinc strengthen the infant’s immune system.

items.title: Optimal growth
items.content: Balanced proteins, fats, and carbs provide the calories needed for healthy growth.

items.title: Hypoallergenic
items.content: Hydrolyzed proteins lower the risk of allergic reactions in sensitive babies.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Despite hydrolysis, some infants may still react to casein or whey.

items.title: Incorrect reconstitution
items.content: Over‑concentrated formula can strain kidneys; overly diluted formula may not meet energy needs.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: If the container is not kept dry, the powder can absorb moisture and spoil.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: The formula contains lactose; infants with lactose intolerance need an alternative.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Mix the specified amount of powder with pre‑warmed (about 37 °C) baby water. Stir thoroughly until smooth, let stand for 1–2 minutes, then check temperature before feeding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry powder in its original packaging in a cool, dry place away from direct light. Use within 30 days after opening. Prepared formula can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours and should be warmed to room temperature before feeding.

content.title: About
content.content: Dried persimmon is made from fully ripe persimmon fruits (Diospyros kaki) that are peeled and dehydrated until the moisture content drops, preserving most of the fruit’s nutrients. The result is a sweet, slightly caramel‑like flavor with a soft, chewy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Persimmon originates from East Asia but is now cultivated in the Mediterranean, the United States and South America.
In Japan dried persimmon, called “hosho,” is traditionally served during tea ceremonies.
Drying concentrates the natural sugars, making dried persimmon sweeter than the fresh fruit.
The orange hue comes from high levels of carotenoids.
Dried persimmon has been used for centuries in Asian desserts and as a natural sweetener.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: Persimmon supplies potassium, magnesium and iron, important for heart health and blood formation.

items.title: Moderate glycemic impact
items.content: When dried, the fruit raises blood sugar more slowly than many other sweet snacks, making it a reasonable option for controlled carbohydrate intake.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Dried persimmon is calorie‑dense and can spike blood glucose if eaten in large amounts.

items.title: Allergy potential
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to persimmon.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large servings may cause bloating due to the fruit’s fiber load.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy dried persimmon as a snack, toss it into oatmeal, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or use it to make sauces and jams. Soaking it briefly in warm water can re‑hydrate the pieces for a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried persimmon in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to 12 months. Discard any pieces that develop mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork tenderloin is a lean, tender cut taken from the inner side of the pig’s backbone. It contains very little fat, has a delicate texture and a mild flavor. Tenderloin is commonly roasted, pan‑seared, grilled, or sliced into medallions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tenderloin is one of the leanest pork cuts, with about 5 % fat.
In ancient cultures it was considered a delicacy and served at special feasts.
When cooked properly it stays juicy despite its low fat content.
It is often marinated in soy sauce, honey, and spices to boost flavor.
In the United States it is frequently called “tenderloin roast” and used for pork tenderloin medallions.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides roughly 22 g of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Its low fat content makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which support metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides zinc, iron and phosphorus, important for immunity, blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Contains creatine
items.content: Creatine in meat can help improve muscular strength and endurance.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked pork may harbor Salmonella or Trichinella. Cook to an internal temperature of 63 °C (145 °F).

items.title: Sodium in processed versions
items.content: Marinated or smoked tenderloin can be high in salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout should limit tenderloin because purines can raise uric acid levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tenderloin can be roasted whole, sliced into steaks or medallions, pan‑seared, grilled, or baked. A simple rub of olive oil, garlic, rosemary and lemon juice enhances flavor. Avoid overcooking; aim for a pink center, then let rest 5–10 minutes before slicing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tenderloin in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C in an airtight container for 2–3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen pieces in the fridge before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup NFS (product code 3905) is a ready‑to‑eat dry soup developed by NFS. It consists of dehydrated vegetables, spices and flavor enhancers that form a tasty, nutritious meal when rehydrated with hot water.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soup NFS is available in more than 20 flavors, ranging from classic chicken to spicy Asian blends.
Each serving provides about 200 kcal, making it a convenient quick‑meal option.
The product is gluten‑free and suitable for people with gluten intolerance.
The rapid‑drying process preserves a high level of vitamins in the ingredients.
Packaging is made from recyclable material to reduce environmental impact.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup contains vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Legumes and grains provide about 8 g of protein per serving.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Dehydrated vegetables add fiber that aids normal digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The soup contains virtually no saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Electrolytes
items.content: Potassium and sodium are present to help maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: The soup may contain soy protein, dairy powders or nut‑derived flavorings—check labels if you have allergies.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some flavors have elevated salt levels; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Requires hot water
items.content: Proper preparation needs water at least 90 °C.

items.title: Possible gluten in certain flavors
items.content: While most variants are gluten‑free, a few may contain wheat in spice mixes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour 250 ml of boiling water over the soup, cover, and let it stand for 3–5 minutes. Optionally add fresh vegetables, herbs, or cooked meat pieces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the package tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Tortellini are small ring-shaped pasta filled with creamy cheese. This version is served without sauce, allowing the delicate flavor of the cheese and the texture of the dough to shine. The pasta is traditionally made from eggs and high‑quality flour, and the filling may include ricotta, Parmesan, and other soft cheeses.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortellini originate from Italy; the name comes from the verb “torcere” meaning “to twist,” describing their shape.
The cheese filling makes them a good source of calcium and protein.
Although often served in broth, sauce‑free tortellini retain a lighter, airier texture.
They are traditionally handcrafted, but modern production often uses automated lines.
Italy celebrates a “Tortellini Festival” dedicated to this beloved dish.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The cheese filling provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium that supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Dairy in the filling is a good source of vitamin B12, important for the nervous system.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Sauce‑free tortellini contain virtually no sugar, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Whole‑wheat flour used in the dough adds a modest amount of iron.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cheese filling may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to milk proteins.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cheese‑filled tortellini are relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese can contain notable amounts of salt, which is relevant for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauce‑free tortellini can be enjoyed on their own, added to a light broth, or sprinkled with fresh herbs and grated Parmesan. They reheat well in the microwave or steamed, preserving their tender texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry tortellini in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked tortellini can be kept in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. When frozen, they remain good for up to 3 months.
